original-data.t: The six customers with their two original features. We will compress them to one number each, then measure **exactly what was lost**.

pc1-pc2.t: **PC1** (yellow) follows the trend and **PC2** (blue, dashed) is perpendicular to it. Together they describe the same points in rotated axes.

variance-bars.t: PC1 carries **6.03 of the 6.20 total (97.2%)** and PC2 carries **0.17 (2.8%)**. A component's explained-variance ratio is its eigenvalue divided by the total.

keep-both.t: With **k = 2** we keep both coordinates: **Z = Xc V** is the same data in rotated axes, so **100%** of the variance is kept.

drop-pc2.t: Keeping **k = 1** discards the PC2 coordinates, the short red segments (**0.13, 0.23, −0.43, 0.43, −0.61, 0.24**). These are exactly the information we choose to throw away.

projected-representation.t: Each customer is now just its **PC1 coordinate z**, shown as a dot on the line. The faded originals show what we started from.

reconstruct.t: Mapping each z back with **x̂ = mean + z·v₁** places a hollow ring on the PC1 line. Each ring is near its original customer but not exactly on it.

reconstruction-error.t: The red segments from each original to its ring are the error. Their squared lengths add up to **0.863 = 5 × 0.1725**, exactly the variance we dropped.

explained-variance.t: PC1 keeps **97.2%** of the variance and loses **2.8%**. This measures how much spread is retained. It is **not** a prediction accuracy.

tradeoff-summary.t: More components keep more variance but cost more size. **95% explained variance is not 95% accuracy:** the discarded part could hold what a later task needs, so always check the downstream result.
